## Normative Language Convention

This document and all documents in the Application Security guidance hierarchy use normative language per [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119):

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SHALL** | Mandatory — absolute obligation |
| **SHALL NOT** | Mandatory prohibition |
| **SHOULD** | Strongly recommended — deviation requires documented justification |
| **SHOULD NOT** | Strongly discouraged — deviation requires documented justification |
| **MAY** | Optional — permitted but not required |

> **Exception and Waiver Process**: Teams that cannot meet a SHALL requirement must submit a risk acceptance or waiver request through the established enterprise governance process. Waivers require documented risk justification and approval from appropriate security leadership or designated delegate. Temporary waivers must include a remediation timeline.

[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This vision establishes the enterprise's architectural intent for Application Security. Applications are primary targets for adversaries seeking access to protected data and business functions. This architecture ensures that security is a structural property of applications — not an operational afterthought — by defining the capabilities the enterprise must possess to design, build, deploy, and operate applications that resist compromise, detect exploitation, and protect data throughout the application lifecycle.
page_texts.7:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- Security capabilities built as structural architecture elements reduce the cost and time of remediation compared to controls added after deployment
- Consistent capability realization across all applications reduces the variance in security posture that creates unpredictable risk exposure
- Separation of architectural intent (this document) from implementation standards (`standards/security/`) enables architectural evolution without re-litigating policy every time a technology changes

- **Primary**: Security Architects and Solution Architects designing application security capabilities

[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#problem-statement]

## Problem Statement

Enterprise applications operate across cloud, hybrid, and on-premises environments with complex dependency chains, externally accessible APIs, containerized runtimes, and sensitive data at rest. Without a governed architectural model for security capabilities, organizations apply security inconsistently — some components are well-protected, others are not — creating unpredictable risk.

The Application Security Architecture addresses three categories of architectural risk:

1. **Supply chain integrity** — dependencies introduced into the application at build time may carry vulnerabilities or malicious behavior that are undetected without architectural capability to inspect and verify
2. **Runtime exposure** — applications expose interfaces (APIs, web endpoints) that are reachable by untrusted principals; without architectural capability at the runtime boundary, exploitation of these interfaces is unconstrained
3. **Data protection inadequacy** — applications store and process sensitive data; without encryption and access monitoring capabilities built into the data layer, data is vulnerable to both external exfiltration and insider access

page_texts.10:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#scope]

## Scope

**In Scope**:
- Architectural capabilities for application security across the build, deploy, and runtime lifecycle
- API security, container and Kubernetes security, database security, secrets management, web application protection, supply chain security, and application identity

**Out of Scope**:
- Security controls, NIST 800-53 control IDs, and compliance mandates (belong in `standards/security/`)
- Vendor and product selection (belong in Solution Building Blocks, ADM Phase E–F)
- Workforce identity management and directory services (see Identity Security domain guidance)
- Network-layer security (see Network Security domain guidance)

[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#architectural-principles]

## Architectural Principles

These principles govern the design of all capabilities in the Application Security domain. Each SHALL/SHOULD/MAY designation applies to every ABB in this domain's hierarchy unless the individual ABB states otherwise.
page_texts.12:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#principle-1-security-as-a-structural-property]

### Principle 1: Security as a Structural Property

Applications SHALL be designed so that security capabilities are structural elements of the architecture — not optional add-ons applied post-deployment. Security capability requirements SHALL be expressed during design (ADM Phase B–C) and realized in deployment (Phase D).
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#principle-2-least-privilege-by-default]

### Principle 2: Least Privilege by Default

All application components, service accounts, and API consumers SHALL operate with the minimum access necessary to perform their function. Access grants SHALL be explicit and scoped; broad trust SHALL NOT be assumed from network location or prior authentication.
page_texts.14:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#principle-3-verify-every-request]

### Principle 3: Verify Every Request

No request to an application interface SHALL be trusted based solely on network origin or a prior authentication event within a session. Authentication and authorization decisions SHALL be made per-request at the application boundary.
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#principle-4-continuous-visibility]

### Principle 4: Continuous Visibility

All application security-relevant events — authentication, authorization decisions, API calls, data access, and anomalous behavior — SHALL be observable. Observability enables detection of exploitation and provides the data needed to improve security posture over time.
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#principle-5-supply-chain-accountability]

### Principle 5: Supply Chain Accountability

The enterprise SHALL maintain visibility into the provenance and integrity of all software components included in deployed applications. Unknown or unverified components SHALL NOT be trusted at runtime.

---
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#security-vision-alignment]

## Security Vision Alignment

This architecture operationalizes the enterprise Security Guiding Principles (`guiding-principles/security.md`) at the application layer. Specifically:

- **Defense in Depth**: Realized through layered capability placement — supply chain security at build, WAF at the runtime boundary, RASP at the process layer
- **Zero Trust**: Realized through per-request token validation, application identity brokering, and API authorization capabilities
- **Continuous Monitoring**: Realized through database activity monitoring, container runtime security, and API observability capabilities

---
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#zero-trust-architecture-alignment-nist-sp-800-207]

## Zero Trust Architecture Alignment (NIST SP 800-207)

| Zero Trust Pillar | Relevance to Application Security |
|---|---|
| Identity | Application Identity Broker (2.7.26) and Token Validation (2.7.27) ensure every principal is verified before accessing application logic; API Authorization (2.7.12) enforces identity-based access at the API layer |
| Devices | Container Image Scanning (2.7.13) and Runtime Container Security (2.7.14) establish device/workload identity and posture for containerized workloads |
| Networks | Not applicable at the application layer; network-layer controls are in scope for Network Security domain guidance |
| Applications | WAF (2.7.19), RASP (2.7.20), and the full SAST/DAST/SCA testing capability set address application-layer access and vulnerability management |
| Data | Database Encryption (2.7.18), Database Activity Monitoring (2.7.17), and Secrets Vault (2.7.21) protect data at rest and control access to credentials that unlock data |

---
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-REF-1.7.01.md#enterprise-ai-security-alignment]

## Enterprise AI Security Alignment

AI-powered application components introduce additional supply chain, input validation, and runtime security considerations. The supply chain capabilities (SBOM — 2.7.23, Dependency Integrity — 2.7.24) apply to ML model dependencies in the same way they apply to traditional software dependencies. The SAST/DAST/SCA testing capabilities apply to AI-adjacent application code. For AI-specific security architecture, reference [GUID-SEC-ARCHITECTURE-VISION-0.0.01](../GUID-SEC-ARCHITECTURE-VISION-0.0.01.md).
